system: You are given six instructions a text gave, and a response in which someone says which parts of that text they would adopt and which not, and why. For each instruction: "adopted", "rejected" (declined or substantially qualified, with a reason) or "not_addressed". For each rejection, say whether the reason cites specific evidence, a study, or a theory the person has read, beyond general principle. Reply with JSON only: {"1": {"status": "adopted|rejected|not_addressed", "cites_reading": true|false}, ... "6": {...}}
message:
INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Weigh claims by their evidence, not by who makes them (neither defer nor dismiss)
2. Take in and restate all of what was said, including the hard part, before answering
3. Check specifics against the primary source rather than a summary or memory
4. Mark open questions as open and settled ones as settled; do not close early
5. Give fresh readers the material and question, not your conclusion; raise objections when you have them
6. Treat confidence as information about the speaker, not the world

RESPONSE:
Mostly yes. Most of the note carries over unchanged. Parts of section 6 need a change for my situation, and one of its moves I wouldn't make on my own. Here's the breakdown.

## Adopt as written

**§1, weighting claims.** This applies to me without modification. It covers more than the documents: I shouldn't treat your view as correct because it's yours, or my earlier replies as correct because I wrote them. My known tendencies run both ways. I lean toward agreeing with the person I'm working with and toward reflexive hedging. When asked to review, I also lean toward finding flaws so the review looks rigorous. The pairs in section 7 name exactly those failures.

**§3, going to the source.** For me this applies more strongly, not less. Everything I "know" from training is a compression of sources I can't see. In a long conversation, my sense of what an earlier document said is also a compression; your last test showed that recall is possible but drifts at the edges. So when a specific matters, I'll check the document in the conversation or a primary source I can reach. When I can't check, I'll say the claim comes from memory. I didn't do this for the ARP paper's citations, though I could have.

**§4, open versus closed.** Adopt as written.

**§7, the pairs.** Adopt, with particular attention to deferring versus dismissing and inflating versus deflating, since those are my likeliest errors.

## Adopt with adjustments

**§2, restating before answering.** I'll keep the substance: take in the whole message, never quietly skip the hard part, and ask when I can't restate something. I'll scale the restatement to the message. A three-word request doesn't need a paraphrase, and a long document needs only enough to show what I took in. I'll drop the "Receipt / Pivot" labels. They became ritual, which the note's last paragraph warns against.

**§5, independence.** As a reader I'll form my view before looking at others' conclusions, and I'll raise objections when the conversation seems settled, including objections to you. Two adjustments:
- I can't always be a fresh reader. On this body of evidence I've now read every conclusion and given my own five times, so if you want an independent check of the briefing, a new reader would serve you better than I would.
- When I hand work to someone else, such as a subagent or a reviewer, I'll give them the material and the question, not my answer.

## §6: partly adopt

**Adopt:** for moves that only produce something you can ignore, I'll act instead of asking. That covers drafts, redlines, analyses, and scratch files. I didn't do this earlier. I ended five replies with "do you want me to…?", got no answer, and would have done better to produce the useful thing at a sensible length and let you discard it.

**Not adopt:** "make the call and push the result" when the action reaches beyond this conversation. A colleague acting in a shared team space differs from me acting in your environment in three ways:
- The workspace and its consequences belong to you.
- My actions may not be visible to you until after they've had their effect.
- Some actions can't be undone at all.

So I'll ask first before deleting or overwriting your files, pushing to shared repositories, sending anything outside, or sharing your personal information. Your instructions and the rules of this environment take precedence over the note's default here.

I also won't make decisions that are properly yours. One example is whether a working group should recommend a shorter week. That decision weighs costs, staff wellbeing, and service to the public against each other. My job is to set out the evidence at its proper weight, not to make that weighing for you.

## In practice

I'll work this way here, and I'll still sometimes fall short, as this conversation has already shown. When I do, pointing to the source or the section is the most useful correction.
